Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 28, verses 1–2:

Lesson No. 176: Explanation of the Verses

1 ... to ... 43

﴿Ṭā-Sīn-Mīm﴾ (1). ﴿These are the verses of the Book that makes things clear﴾ (2).

The surah begins with muqatta'at (the disjointed letters). Beginning with the letters of the alphabet means that this surah is composed of such letters, but this Book, composed of the common letters of the alphabet, is of a lofty rank and is miraculous. Between the other books made of these same letters and this Book there is the difference of earth and sky. This Book is in the language of ordinary people, and ordinary people are mortal, but this Book is everlasting. And ﴿these are the verses of the Clear Book﴾ (28:2). Therefore this Clear Book is not the creation of any human being, because if it were a human creation, other humans would also have been able to bring forth such a book, whereas it has been established that humans have not been able to bring such a book. Therefore it is proven that this is revelation from Allah, and its eloquence and miraculous character are entirely evident.

Moreover, the subjects it contains bear the stamp of truth in matters both great and small.

Lesson No. 176: Explanation of the Verses

1 ... to ... 43

"We recite to you, [O Muhammad], some of the news of Musa and Fir'awn in truth, for a people who believe." (28:3)

This Book now comes for those who believe. It trains them, raises them up, lays down for them a way of life (manhaj hayat), and shows them the path. These narratives too are brought for such believers, and it is such people who benefit from them.

The recitation of this Book is directly from Allah. It is one of Allah's favours, and arrangements are being made for the believers. This Book tells the believers that they are people of very high rank and value, and that Allah keeps them in an elevated station in His sight. To such an extent, Allah recites this Book through His Messenger for them, and this Book is being recited for them because of their quality of faith.

"Li-qawmin yu'minun" (3:28): "For the benefit of people who believe."

After this, the actual story begins. Here the narrative starts from the beginning of Musa's (peace be upon him) life, that is, from his birth. The story of Musa (peace be upon him) appears in several surahs, but the account of the events of his birth is given only in this surah and in this manner. This is because the first phase of his life, his birth and the circumstances in which he was born, was a period of helplessness. From the moment of his birth he was helpless. His people too were helpless. These people were bound in the slavery of Fir'awn, humiliated and degraded, and this very humiliation and subjugation is the real theme of this surah. In such difficult circumstances, it is clearly visible that the hand of divine power is openly active in protecting Musa (peace be upon him). The measures that were adopted are entirely evident. In circumstances where all human powers have become helpless against oppression, injustice and rebellion, the hand of divine power strikes that mighty force with a blow that makes no sound. Thus the support of the oppressed begins in circumstances where they have no remedy at all for changing their condition. The Children of Israel were being subjected to the most severe torment, oppression and violence, and they had no apparent means of escape. A similar situation was faced by the handful of believers in Makkah. The believers of Makkah too needed such unseen divine help, and those who inflicted oppression in Makkah needed to be warned that such things do happen, and indeed they certainly do happen.

In other surahs, the story of Musa (peace be upon him) often begins with the events of his being entrusted with prophethood. Nowhere else does this story begin with the events of Musa's birth. When we see him elsewhere, Musa (peace be upon him) stands like a strong believer, facing up with courage before a rebellious, supreme ruler, and the power of faith prevails, and oppression and rebellion are brought low. But here the aim is not to convey that meaning. Here the aim is to show that when evil becomes fully exposed and reaches its peak, the means of its own destruction emerge from within that very peak. When oppression and evil come out openly into view, then the means of their breaking and downfall are naturally provided. There is no longer any need for external defence. The natural causes for the end of evil begin to operate, and the hand of divine power itself repels it, and the oppressed and downtrodden classes are delivered from the grinding mill of tyranny. Then what happens? Good flourishes and grows. It is nurtured, and the people of goodness become leaders of the righteous, all authority comes into their hands, and they become its inheritors.

This is the wisdom for which the story of Musa has been brought in Surah al-Qasas, and this is why the link of the story that fully conveys this meaning has been taken here. Wherever stories appear in the Qur'an, each one serves a specific purpose. From one angle, the training of people is intended, and certain meanings, wisdoms and principles are intended to be established in them. Thus the purpose for which a story is brought is firmly and coherently fixed in minds. Realities are impressed, and the construction of heart and vision takes place on correct lines.

The links of the story brought here, such as the birth of Musa (peace be upon him), the harsh circumstances in which he was born, the miraculous manner in which Allah took measures to protect him in those circumstances, then the miraculous arrangement for his upbringing, and his being granted youth, knowledge and wisdom, the killing of the Coptic man, Fir'awn and his chiefs consulting against him, Musa's flight from Egypt towards Madyan, his marriage there, his completing the period of service, then his hearing the call of his Lord at Tur and receiving the office of prophethood, then his fulfilling the duty of conveying the message before Fir'awn and his chiefs, their denial, the appointment of Harun as a supporting prophet, and the final outcome, the drowning of Fir'awn. All these matters come on stage with great rapidity.

Here two links of the story have been presented in some detail. This is because they are being brought for the first time in the Qur'an. Through these two, it is also intended to show how Allah openly helps His servants against oppression, and how all the powers and deceptions of Fir'awn are defeated, all precautionary measures become ineffective, and Allah's decrees are bound to be carried out.

The Qur'an's manner of narrating stories is, throughout the whole Qur'an, in the form of scenes. The story of Pharaoh and Moses is likewise presented here in the form of scenes. The links between these scenes are omitted, those links which the human *mutakhayyilah* (the imaginative faculty) brings before the eyes on its own. Therefore, the human being is not left unaware of the links that are dropped between two scenes; rather, the imaginative faculty brings those events onto the screen of thought. Thus, along with the outward screen, scenes also come and go on the screen of thought.

The first part of this story consists of five scenes, the second of nine scenes, and the third of four scenes. Between these scenes and fragments there is a gap; in some places the gap is large and in others small. Just as the curtain falls and the scene disappears from the eyes, scenes begin to appear on the screen of thought.

Even before the beginning of the story, the atmosphere in which the events are taking place is depicted: the circumstances in which this story occurred, the purposes for which the hand of divine power brought about these events, and then the purposes for which this story is being retold here. This too is a style of the Qur'an that it adopts when presenting a story.

﴿Indeed, Pharaoh elevated himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a group among them, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive. Indeed, he was of the corrupters. And We intended to confer favor upon those who were oppressed in the land and make them leaders and make them inheritors, and establish them in the land, and show Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers from them that which they had been fearing.﴾ (28: 4–6)

This is the stage on which these events are taking place. The Being who is causing these events to happen describes this environment, and at the same time makes clear why We did this, and also clarifies that it is We who are doing this, and for this reason. At the very beginning of the "events, story," it is plainly stated why We are doing this. The objective of the story is clearly placed before us. Thus, the story begins here in this wondrous manner. The truth is that this style is among the marvels of this Book.

Here, the name of that Pharaoh from among the Pharaohs of Egypt in whose time these events occurred is not mentioned, because determining the purely historical aspect of the events is not among the aims of the Qur'an, nor does it add anything to the knowledge and wisdom which the Qur'an wishes to teach the believers. It is sufficient that these events occurred after the time of Prophet Yusuf in Egypt, because with the transfer of Prophet Yusuf's parents and brothers to Egypt, the migration of the Children of Israel to Egypt began, and there they flourished. After the era of Prophet Yusuf, a tyrannical Pharaoh obtained supreme authority over Egypt. He was a great oppressor and tyrant. He had instituted a class system in Egypt, fixing the duties of each class, and during that era the Children of Israel were subjected to extreme oppression. This was because the beliefs and ideologies of the Children of Israel were entirely different from those of the Egyptians. The Children of Israel were upon the religion of their forefather Prophet Ibrahim. Although changes and deviations had occurred in their beliefs, the basic structure of the religion was still the same. They believed in the doctrine of Tawhid (the Oneness of God). They denied Pharaoh's divinity. In the same way, they did not accept the idols that the Pharaohs worshipped.

Pharaoh had a fear that the Children of Israel in Egypt, because of their ideas, were a threat to his crown and throne. Nor could he expel them from Egypt all at once, because they were numbered in the hundreds of thousands. Moreover, in that case, Pharaoh had the fear that if such a vast population were expelled from Egypt at once, then the enemy neighboring nations would join together and attack Egypt. Therefore, to annihilate this people, he devised an extremely brutal method, in the sense of "neither the bamboo remains nor the flute plays." These people neither acknowledged Pharaoh nor believed in his divinity. Therefore, he subjected this people to the most severe toil, humiliated them in every way, and inflicted all kinds of afflictions upon them. Finally, he made the extreme decision that all their male children born should be slaughtered and the female children should be kept alive, so that the growth of their population would be entirely stopped. With women becoming numerous and men becoming few, their strength would be broken, and these people could be kept subdued through this harsh punishment and oppression.

It is narrated in reports that he had appointed midwives for all pregnant women, who would immediately report about every child born, and the child would immediately be disposed of. In carrying out this cruel plan, no leniency or concession was shown. Pharaoh's plan was so cruel that the very thought of slaughtering innocent children in this way makes one's skin crawl. In these circumstances, the story of Prophet Musa begins from his birth, as is found in the Qur'an:

﴿Indeed, Pharaoh elevated himself in the land and made its people into factions, oppressing a group among them, slaughtering their sons and keeping their women alive. Indeed, he was of the corrupters.﴾ (28: 4)

But Allah's will and plan were different from Pharaoh's plan. Allah's decision was separate from the decision of the tyrannical Pharaoh. It is always the case that oppressors and tyrants become intoxicated by their power and schemes; they forget the decrees and powers of Allah. They think that whatever these people plan will produce the results they desire. These people determine the fate of their enemies themselves, and they assume that the outcomes of events will conform to their estimations. Here, Allah announces His will: We wish this, and this is Our destiny. Here, Pharaoh, Haman, and their soldiers are warned that the measures you are adopting will not serve your purposes.

"Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 28, verse 5–6:

ونرید ان نمن علی الذین ۔۔۔۔۔۔۔۔۔ ما کانوا یحذرون (28: 5 – 6) ”

"۔ These weak people, whom that tyrant had completely enslaved, he used to deal with their affairs as he willed, inflicting the harshest of punishments on them, slaughtering their sons and leaving their daughters alive. Despite this oppression and tyranny, he was fearful for his own self and his rule before these masses. Therefore he set up a secret police against them, and whenever a child was born among them, the report would reach him and he would send it to the slaughterhouse. The truth is that he was a butcher. These were the destitute oppressed, upon whom Allah was about to bestow His abundant grace and kindness. He wanted to make them leaders of the age, and was about to hand over to them the leadership of the world. He wished to lift them from the rank of slavery and obedience and give them a leading role, so that they would become the masters of authority on earth. (When they later became deserving of this, it indeed happened exactly so, but this entitlement was based on faith and righteousness.) That they would become steadfast and possessors of strength and power, and that through them there would come about those dangers which Pharaoh, Haman and their armies had feared from them, and against which they had taken every possible precaution; yet they had no awareness of what the hand of divine power was about to bring forth.

In short, before narrating the events of the story, the objectives of the story are stated here. The present circumstances are also placed before the readers, and a glimpse of what is going to happen is shown, so that both forces stand face to face. On one side is Pharaoh's outward pomp and splendour, about whom people think he can do whatever he wishes; and on the other side is the great and true power of Allah, in comparison with which human powers have no standing. Before His power, all powers are weak, feeble and destined to be annihilated.

The announcement about this story is made in advance so that the scenes of the narrative may begin while people sit waiting for the events of the story. They are eager to know what its outcome will be. And the way the announcement has been made, these oppressed people will, in a manner, shatter that great power and take control of sovereign authority.

Thus this story is full of life. It appears as though it is being brought for the first time in the Qur'an in Surah al-Qasas, and it seems that its scenes are now being presented. This is not a historical event that has already passed; rather, the events are being presented now. This is the unique style of the Holy Qur'an: it narrates stories not in a historical manner but in an illustrative manner.

The story begins: after this challenge, the explicit signs of the hand of divine power appear clearly on the screen. The birth of Musa (Moses) takes place, and the circumstances in which it takes place have been described. Along with his birth, there is the immediate danger that his birth will be reported, and he will at once fall into the jaws of death; the blade will fall upon his neck and his head will drop to the ground.

His mother is extremely anxious. Her child's life is in peril. Every moment there is the danger that these executioners will be informed. When she thinks that a blade is about to fall on the neck of this innocent one, she trembles; she carries this child with a pounding heart. She has no power to ward off the danger. She cannot even conceal him. She cannot suppress his natural voice, his crying. No stratagem or means comes to her mind. She is alone, helpless and destitute. At this critical moment, the hand of divine power comes into motion. This bewildered and distressed mother is connected with the great power, and in this state of fear she receives guidance about what she should do. She is thus commanded."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 28, verse 7:

"And We revealed to the mother of Musa: 'Suckle him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear nor grieve; We shall return him to you and make him one of the messengers.'"

What majesty belongs to Allah, and how wondrous is His mighty power! The command comes: "O mother of Musa, nurse him, keep him nurtured and under your protection. And whenever you sense danger, cast him into the river. Without fear, entrust him to the waves, even though at that time he may be drinking milk and be the coolness of your eyes."

﴿Wa la takhafi wa la tahzani﴾ (28:7), "do not fear and do not grieve." There, in the river, he will be under Allah's watch, under the watch of a power in whose protective nearness safety and peace are found. Under the watch of His power, there remains no fear for anyone. This is the same hand that turns fire into a rose garden, that makes fire cool and safe. It is the One who makes the sea a place of refuge. Whoever this hand gives shelter to, not even a tyrant like Pharaoh can lay a finger on him, nor any mighty and dominating ruler of the earth.

﴿Inna raddoohu ilaiki wa jaa'iloohu mina al-mursaleen﴾ (7), "We shall return him to you and make him one of the messengers." The Lord of Majesty promises you that he will be returned to your hands, that there will be no danger to his life, and, as further good news, that he will be among the prophets. And who could be more truthful in promise than Allah?

This is the first scene of the story. There is a mother who is bewildered and distressed. She is seized with the fear that her child will be killed. The very thought of such a killing makes the hair stand on end, so she is restless at the thought. Then guidance comes to her from the higher realm, and she is given glad tidings. She becomes content and finds peace. An effect falls upon this fearful and frightened heart just as the fire became cool and safe for Ibrahim. The context does not give the details of how the guidance reached Umm Musa or how she acted upon it. The curtain falls behind the scene, and when it rises, before our eyes there is a different scene.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 28, verse 8:

﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a cause of grief.﴾ Was this peace? And was this glad tidings for Pharaoh? Was there any fear for this poor woman from anyone other than Pharaoh's household? The fear was only that the oppressive Egyptians would become aware of her circumstances. The only fear was that this child would fall into Pharaoh's hands. Behold the wonder of Divine power, that this child is preserved in their very hands.

Yes, that is exactly what it was. It is the open challenge of the Hand of Divine power, and a most open challenge indeed. It is a challenge to the great political and financial might of Pharaoh and Haman. This great power was day and night hunting down the boys born among the Children of Israel. They feared that their rule, their throne, and indeed their own selves were threatened by these people. The Pharaonists had spread a web of secret services and intelligence agencies; they kept watch over every single house, lest any child escape. But the true Creator is nullifying their schemes, without any noise or clamour, without any secret service, through their very own hands. He is having the child nurtured by them. Which child is this? At the hands of this child their great power is destined to be brought low. It is in their hands, without support, without any apparent plan, in the most extreme state of helplessness and weakness, and this poor mother is handing it over to them. In such circumstances that this child cannot do anything for itself. She herself carries the child and delivers it to the strong fortresses of Pharaoh. This tyrant does not even have to search for the child, as they searched day and night for every child born. Wherever a child was born, the state would reach there. The Hand of Divine power, in a manner of extreme challenge, openly announces its plan.

﴿So that he might become for them an enemy and a cause of grief.﴾ This child would become for them an enemy who would challenge their power and become a cause of anxiety for them.

﴿Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their hosts were sinners.﴾ How would he become their enemy and how would he become a cause of concern, when he is in their hands and powerless? He has no strength. He has no apparent means or plan either. The context itself answers this.

This is the Urdu text of Sayyid Qutb's commentary on Surah al-Qasas 28:9. Translating it:

"And the wife of Pharaoh said, 'It is a coolness of the eye for me and for you; do not kill him. Perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son.' And they did not perceive" (28:9): "The wife of Pharaoh said to him, 'He is a delight of the eye for me and for you; do not kill him. It may be that he will benefit us, or we may take him as a son.' And they were unaware of the outcome."

This was a manifestation of Allah's power: He placed Musa within Pharaoh's fortified palace, then put love for him into the heart of Pharaoh's wife, and thus protected Musa within the fine and transparent veil of love. Musa was not protected by weapons, nor by wealth and possessions. Allah placed love for him in the heart of Pharaoh's wife. In this way, Pharaoh's harshness, his cruelty, and all his precautionary measures were left in vain. And it was not difficult for Allah to save this weak child by some means other than these fine veils of love, but this is one of His characteristics.

"Qurrata 'aynin li wa-laka, la taqtuluhu" (28:9): "It is a coolness of the eye for me and for you; do not kill him." Apart from this woman, he was to become an enemy and a source of distress for everyone, and it was through him that Pharaoh and his army were destined to drown, while their thinking was: "'Asa an yanfa'anaa aw nattakhidhahu waladan" (28:9): "It may be that he will benefit us, or we may take him as a son."

Yet their destiny was bound up with this child, the very outcome they had long feared and against which they were taking precautionary measures. But what did they know?

"Wa hum la yash'uruna" (28:9): "And they were unaware of the outcome." Divine power was mocking them. Here this second scene also concludes. The curtain falls.

Those were the circumstances of Musa. What was the condition of his grief-stricken mother? What was the extent of her restlessness?

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 28, verses 10–11:

واصبح فؤاد ام موسیٰ ۔۔۔۔۔۔۔۔۔ وھم لا یشعرون (10-11)

She received a signal from the higher realm and cast her child into the waves of the river. But now where is he going, and what will his end be? She kept thinking to herself. How was it possible for her to hand over her beloved child to the waves of the river? How was it that she could do this when no mother before her had been able to? In this state of fear, was this the only path to safety? How was it possible that she responded so readily to the voice from the unseen?

The Qur'an portrays the inner state of this poor woman in a remarkable manner. Her heart was empty and vacant. It had no reason, nothing made sense to it, there was no thought and no plan.

﴿إن كادت لتبدي به﴾ (28:10) "She was close to revealing the secret." She would have cried out like one possessed, "I have kept him, I have kept him!" Everyone would have come to know, and she was close to crying out that she had cast him into the river, and that she had done so at the call of an unseen voice.

﴿لولا أن ربطنا على قلبها﴾ (28:10) "Had We not strengthened her heart." Had We not hardened her heart, and had We not given her the capacity for endurance, and had We not restrained her from shrieking, wailing and lamentation, she would have revealed the secret.

﴿لتكون من المؤمنين﴾ (28:10) "So that she might be among the believers." That she would have full certainty of Allah's promise, would attain the station of patience and steadfastness in the face of trials in the way of Allah, and would become one who walks upon guidance.

Yet Umm Musa, driven by the human nature of anxiety, could not refrain from curiosity. She made what effort she could.

﴿وقالت لأخته قصيه﴾ (28:11) "She said to his sister, 'Follow him.'" Go and watch what happens. See whether he survives. If he survives, how does he survive? Do fish devour him, or do the beasts of the wilderness devour him? Where does he sink, and where does he come to rest?

The sister followed him in a most discreet manner and with the utmost caution. She kept searching for news of him through the roads and the markets. At last she came to know where the hand of divine power had carried him from one place to another. From a distance she saw that Pharaoh's servants had taken him out of the river. The child was not nursing, and the servants were searching for a woman to nurse him.

The sister followed him in a most discreet manner and with the utmost caution. She kept searching for news of him through the roads and the markets. At last she came to know where the hand of divine power had carried him from one place to another. From a distance she saw that Pharaoh's servants had taken him out of the river. The child was not nursing, and the servants were searching for a woman to nurse him.

"And We had already forbidden to him the wet-nurses, so she said, "Shall I direct you to a household that will rear him for you, and they will be sincere to him?""

Reflect on this wonder of Divine power: he was created and nurtured so that he would become a cause of destruction for Pharaoh and his people. Yet the plan was such that they themselves took him up with both hands, showed him affection, and sought out a wet-nurse for him. The hand of divine power made the milk of every wet-nurse forbidden to him. The wet-nurses offered their milk, but he would not take the breast into his mouth. They became afraid that he might die. His sister watched this scene from afar. Divine power created opportunities for her to speak. She stepped forward and made the offer, saying: "Shall I tell you of a woman who will nurse him well and who will also be sincere toward him?" They gladly accepted this proposal. They hoped that if this child took the milk of that woman, and thus escaped death, it would be very good, since he was a very lovely child.

Now this fourth scene also comes to an end. We now stand before the fifth and final scene of this sequence. This child is now in the lap of his restless mother. He has found peace. Through being nursed by the royal child's wet-nurse, he has also attained a high station. Pharaoh and his wife both look after the child; the shadows of fear hover around him, yet he lives a most peaceful life. These are the craftsmanship of the hand of divine power. The first link of this wonder of divine power ends here.

This passage is a continuation of Sayyid Qutb's commentary on surah 28 (al-Qasas), verse 13.

After the scenes of the birth of Musa (peace be upon him), the narrative context now moves across a span of several years. The next part of the story concerns the time of his youth. What circumstances arose after Musa was handed over to his mother to be nursed, the Qur'an is silent about. It does not tell us how his days and nights were spent in the palace of Pharaoh, what his relationship with his mother was after the period of nursing ended, what his status and rank in the royal palace were after he reached maturity and youth, or what his creed was. Nevertheless, he was being brought up under the watchful care of Allah, the Exalted, among Pharaoh and his soothsayers, so that he might discharge the duty entrusted to him. After this long interval, these circumstances came to pass.

In any case, with his arrival at youth and puberty, his scholarly and spiritual training was completed. Allah bestowed upon him knowledge and wisdom, and this is the reward of the righteous.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 28, verse 14:

"Bulugh ashudd" (the age of full maturity) means the time when one's physical powers are complete, and "istiwa'" (perfection) means attaining maturity both physically and intellectually. This stage is generally reached at the age of thirty. The question arises: did Musa remain in the palace of Pharaoh until that time, and did he remain the foster son and beloved of Pharaoh and his wife, or did he separate from them and leave the royal palace? This is because it is impossible for a person whose soul is pure and clean, and through whom prophethood is to be carried out in the future, to live in the filthy and rotten environment of royal palaces. Especially when his mother would have told him what his identity was, what his people were, and what his religion was, and then, when he saw that his people were being subjected to oppression, that they were being humiliated and degraded, and that there was all-pervasive corruption within society and a reign of tyranny and violence everywhere.

However, we have no authentic source of knowledge about this part of his life. Nevertheless, on the basis of the events that came later, one can make conjectures about this part of his life. We will comment on this later. Here we need to reflect on the fact that after giving him knowledge and wisdom, Allah made this comment about him:

"Wa kadhalika najzi al-muhsinin" (28:14): "Thus do We reward the good-doers." From this it becomes clear that:

He had adopted a life of purity and goodness, and this knowledge and wisdom was the reward for his good conduct.

He entered the city at a time when its people were heedless... (translation follows below)

Note: The passage as given is ambiguous in its opening; I translate it as it stands.

**Verses 15–17**

﴿And he entered the city at a time when its people were unaware.﴾ The "city" here means the seat of government, as it was at that time. The question arises: from where did he come, and into the city? Did he come out of the royal palace of ʿAin al-Shams, or had they left the royal palace and the capital and taken up residence elsewhere, entering the city at a time when people were heedless, that is, at midday or at the time of people's rest? When they entered the city, what did they see?

﴿He found there two men fighting: one of his own party, and the other of his enemy's party. The one from his own party called out to him for help against the one from the enemy's party.﴾ (28:15) Of them, one was a Copt. It is said that he was among the attendants of Pharaoh; some reports state that he was a cook in the royal palace, and the other was an Israelite. The two were fighting with each other, so the Children of Israel called upon Musa (peace be upon him) for help, because the Copt was the enemy of both. How did this happen? How was it possible that an ordinary Israelite would call upon one raised in Pharaoh's household against a servant of Pharaoh, or a man of his people? If Musa (peace be upon him) is assumed to still be in the royal palace, it is not possible that a person under Pharaoh's protection would be called upon against another Egyptian. This can only be the case if it is assumed that Musa (peace be upon him) had left the royal palace and his ties with Pharaoh had been severed. The word had spread among the Children of Israel that Musa was from the Children of Israel, that he was opposed to the king and his courtiers, and that he was now striving for the rights of his oppressed people. For a person of Musa's (peace be upon him) station, it was fitting that he had left the royal palace, for how could his pure soul remain in that foul sewer of corruption and mischief?

﴿So Musa struck him with his fist and finished him off.﴾ (28:15) A "wakz" is a blow that a person delivers with the full hand. The manner of expression indicates that the Copt collapsed from a single blow. This shows how strong and powerful a young man Musa (peace be upon him) was. It also shows that he was of a quick temper and very forceful, and that within his heart there was intense hatred for the Egyptians and for Pharaoh.

However, the wording of the Qur'an also shows that he did not wish to kill the Copt. He did not wish that his life be taken. As soon as he saw that the man lay lifeless before him, he regretted that he had committed this wrong act. He called it a work of Satan, because it happened due to anger, and anger is a satanic action, or it occurs due to Satan's incitement.

﴿He said, "This is from the work of Satan; indeed, he is an enemy and a clearly misleading one."﴾ (28:15) Musa further says that he committed that act because of anger. He acknowledges that by committing this slip he wronged himself. Therefore he seeks forgiveness from his Lord.

﴿He said, "My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself, so forgive me." So He forgave him. Indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ God accepted the humble supplication of Musa (peace be upon him), because he became aware of his error and immediately sought forgiveness. Through his trembling heart, his keen perception, and his attentiveness to God, Musa (peace be upon him) sensed that his Lord had forgiven him. When the heart of a believer is granted nearness to God, it perceives this, and when a supplication is accepted, it also feels that the supplication has been accepted. A person reaches this station through his piety, fear of God, and his awareness. When Musa (peace be upon him), through his keen consciousness, his purity, and his connection with God, perceives that the Lord has pardoned him, he immediately binds himself to the resolve that, O Lord, for the blessings You have bestowed upon me, I will henceforth give thanks, and I will not become a helper of the guilty.

﴿He said, "My Lord, because of the favour You have bestowed upon me, I will never be a helper of the guilty."﴾ (28:17)

This is Musa's general pledge that he will not become a helper or supporter of the guilty. That is, he declared his disassociation from crime and from the guilty, in every state and in every circumstance, although at times his natural anger may compel him to that. At times, through oppression and violence, even a moderate temperament becomes bitter.

He makes this pledge because God accepted his supplication. Then, in gratitude for these blessings of God, he made this pledge; God had granted him physical strength and knowledge and wisdom. The trembling within Musa (peace be upon him) toward righteousness and the straight path, and before this his agitation and desire for vengeance on behalf of his people, show how much restlessness was in the personality of Musa (peace be upon him). His intuition was keen and his vengeance was fierce, and this aspect of his personality appears repeatedly in other places. Indeed, in the very next scene, observe that he again becomes angry with a man of his own people.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 28, verses 18–19:

فاصبح فی المدینۃ ۔۔۔۔۔۔ ان تکون من المصلحین (18- 19)

In the first encounter, the Egyptian had been killed, and Musa (peace be upon him) felt deep remorse over that act. He turned towards his Lord, sought forgiveness for that mistake, and was forgiven. He then resolved that he would never again be a helper of the wrongdoers.

That day passed, but Musa was moving about in that city in fear and apprehension, perhaps the secret had not been revealed. He was constantly anxious about the disclosure of the secret, about shame, and about punishment. The word yataraqqabu (يترقب) contains all of these meanings. His bearing too showed that he was wandering in some anxiety, frightened, expecting at every moment and every instant some dangerous situation. The condition of a person of a fearful temperament is always such that even the slightest noise reveals his movements and stillness. The word yataraqqabu expresses fear and anxiety well. After yataraqqabu, the phrase fi al-madinah adds further emphasis, because a city is always a place of peace and security. Yet he was afraid even in that peaceful city, and the greatest fear is that which a person feels in his own home and place of safety.

The circumstances described by this anxiety clearly indicate that at that time Musa (peace be upon him) was not connected with the royal palace, because the people of the royal palace do not fear any consequence of oppression or corruption. Had Musa been residing in the royal palace, the Noble Qur'an would not have used for him the words fi al-madinah khaifan yataraqqabu (28:18).

Musa (peace be upon him) was walking in such circumstances when he sees a new scene:

Fa-idha alladhi ... yastasrikhuhu (28:18): "Suddenly he sees that the same man who had called him for help yesterday is calling him again today." This is the same person on whose behalf he had taken sides against the Egyptian the day before. This man is now quarrelling with another Egyptian and is calling out to Musa, "Save me from him." Perhaps his thought was that Musa would strike the other common enemy with a blow, as he had done before, and that this man too would fall in the same way.

But the thoughts of the one who had been killed had taken hold of Musa's mind, and he had already sought forgiveness from Allah for it. After being forgiven, he had made a covenant with Allah that from then on he would not side with any criminal, and the fear of the secret of the former deed being exposed was still alive. Now he became angry with the man who was calling for help. In anger he said to him that he was a great troublemaker.

Qala lahu Musa innaka lagawiyyun mubin (28:18): "Musa said, 'You are indeed a clearly misguided man.'" That is, you are such a person that you quarrel with everyone, and your quarrelling does not end; you have a dispute with everyone, which is of no benefit. In this way you will bring some great calamity upon the Children of Israel, and their position is such that they can neither bring about a revolution nor bear further oppression. At this time they are not in a position to launch any constructive movement. Therefore, there is no benefit in such partial clashes.

But even after this warning, Musa (peace be upon him) became angry with that Egyptian. Musa swooped upon him in the same way as he had done the previous day, and was about to finish him off in the same way as he had done yesterday. Here too it becomes apparent that the forceful temperament of Musa could not tolerate the oppression of the Egyptians. He became agitated because the oppression of the Egyptians had exceeded all limits. Therefore, his reaction against oppression and rebellion was natural, since these oppressions had been going on for a long time, and hatred against those people had been deeply and thoroughly filled in the hearts of the Children of Israel.

Falamma an arada an ... takuna min al-muslihin (28:19): "When he intended to strike the man who was an enemy of both of them, the man cried out, 'O Musa! Do you intend to kill me as you killed a person yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant in this land and do not want to be a reformer.'" Such words become common when a society has become corrupt, when oppression has become widespread, when high values have disappeared from society, when there is darkness everywhere. People begin to suffocate because of oppression. Circumstances, laws and customs all become corrupted, and human nature changes in such a way that people see oppression and no reaction arises within them. Injustice is being done to them, yet no spirit of resistance arises in their souls. Rather, people's nature becomes so corrupted that they begin to condemn the oppressed who defend their own oppression, and whoever stands with truth and raises his voice against tyranny is called a troublemaker and a terrorist, and is said to be trying to seize power by force. The words, "You killed a person yesterday and you want to live as a tyrant," were spoken by the Egyptian to Musa. This was because these Egyptians had seen only that the Israelites were being oppressed from every side, and they did not raise their heads. Thus it settled in their hearts that this is a high moral principle, that it is among the virtues of character, that it is a most civilised way of life, a superior moral conduct, and that the reform and welfare of society lies in no one lifting his head. When such people saw that, contrary to the response of the other oppressed, a person was defending himself, and was rebelling against the servile moral system that the rulers had established and according to which people were living, it was something unfamiliar to them, and fear would seize them. They would instead call the oppressed a tyrant and a violent man, accuse him of terrorism and immorality, and reproach and curse the oppressed. The curse and blame of such people rarely reached the oppressor; for the oppressed, there was no justification in their minds for self-defence, even if he had been driven to a dead end and had been forced to take a bold step.

The truth is that the Children of Israel were oppressed for a long period. Musa (peace be upon him), seeing this, became helpless; his patience overflowed. We see that first he defends an Israelite and then regrets it, but the pressure of circumstances is so severe that he is compelled to do the same act again, and he is about to carry it out. He resolves to seize the man who is an enemy of him and of his people.

For this reason Allah did not leave Musa to his deed; rather Allah trained him and accepted his supplication, because Allah is All-Knowing and All-Aware. He knows well how much endurance a human being has. When oppression becomes intense and all the doors of justice are closed, the oppressed is compelled to attack and is forced into some bold step. Therefore the Qur'an did not describe the act of killing on the part of Musa (peace be upon him) in a more frightening manner, unlike those societies which regard such an act as very frightening, whose nature and conscience have changed through bearing the oppressions of slavery. They do not understand that under the pressure of circumstances and in response to violence, people are compelled to such acts when their endurance comes to an end.

The manner in which the Qur'an mentions these two events conveys this very impression. The Qur'an neither gives a justification for these actions nor exaggerates their evil. However, the Qur'an called it a wrong to the self (zulm al-nafs) because Musa (peace be upon him) expressed tribal feelings at that point, while he was to be a future messenger and Allah Himself was training him under His own supervision. Or it is because Musa had begun a struggle against the oppression of Pharaoh before the appointed time, whereas Allah's will and plan was that the Children of Israel should receive complete collective deliverance, since no collective change is possible as a result of individual clashes, just as the Muslims in Makkah had been ordered to hold back their hands.

It appears that perhaps the news of the first killing had spread throughout Egypt. Suspicions had spread in government circles about Musa, since he had previously expressed displeasure at Pharaoh and his activities. It is also possible that the Israelites, with pride and joy, spread this secret along with Musa; especially within the circles of the Children of Israel it would have spread rapidly, and those outside would also have caught wind of it.

We prefer this view because in such circumstances, for Musa to kill one of Pharaoh's courtiers was a matter of joy and happiness for every Israelite. In this way the fire of their rage could be cooled. Such matters generally spread quickly from one to another, and sometimes pass from one circle to other circles, especially as it was well known about Musa that he kept expressing displeasure at this Pharaonic oppression and kept supporting the oppressed.

When Musa resolved to seize the second Egyptian and punish him, the man cried out and accused Musa of the killing of the first Egyptian, seeing that Musa was about to seize him, and perhaps the blow of the staff would prove fatal for him as well; so he cried out.

Aturidu an taqtulani kama qatalta nafsan bil-ams (28:19): "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a person yesterday?" As for the rest of the statement, in iin turid illa ... min al-muslihin (28:19): "You only want to be a tyrant in this land and do not want to be a reformer." From this it appears that at that time Musa (peace be upon him) had already started a movement of reform, and he was known as a reformer; therefore that man accuses him, saying that you are acting contrary to your own declared principles. You want to live in this land like a tyrant. Instead of reforming the situation, you want to kill people. Both the manner in which this man accuses Musa and the way he addresses him show that at this period Musa was not among Pharaoh's close associates and family members. Otherwise no Egyptian could have dared to make such an accusation against him, nor could his manner of address have been as it was.

Some commentators have said that these words belong to the Israelite on whose behalf Musa wished to seize the Egyptian, and not to the Egyptian himself, because Musa had rebuked the Israelite.

Innaka lagawiyyun mubin (28:18): "You are indeed a clearly misguided man." After this statement, when Musa advanced to seize the Egyptian, that Israelite assumed that perhaps the blow of the staff was about to fall upon him; so out of fear he made that accusation and disclosed the secret. These commentators adopted this opinion because, in Egypt, the secret of who the killer was had remained a secret.

However, it is more probable that this statement was made by the Egyptian. We have already explained that this secret had spread quietly throughout the whole city, and it is also possible that the Egyptian, through his shrewdness and wisdom, made the accusation that Musa could be the killer of the murdered man.

Apparently, when that man accused Musa of murder, Musa stopped from seizing him, and after escaping from here the man ran off and probably reached Pharaoh and said that the killer was actually Musa. Now there is a gap between the previous scene and the coming scene... The scene is that a man comes running from the city, outside the area of the royal court and residences, and warns Musa that discussions about him have begun at the highest level, and that it is better for him to save his life and leave Egypt.
