His bearing too showed that he was wandering in some anxiety, frightened, expecting at every moment and every instant some dangerous situation. The condition of a person of a fearful temperament is always such that even the slightest noise reveals his movements and stillness. The word yataraqqabu expresses fear and anxiety well. After yataraqqabu, the phrase fi al-madinah adds further emphasis, because a city is always a place of peace and security. Yet he was afraid even in that peaceful city, and the greatest fear is that which a person feels in his own home and place of safety.

The circumstances described by this anxiety clearly indicate that at that time Musa (peace be upon him) was not connected with the royal palace, because the people of the royal palace do not fear any consequence of oppression or corruption. Had Musa been residing in the royal palace, the Noble Qur'an would not have used for him the words fi al-madinah khaifan yataraqqabu (28:18).

Musa (peace be upon him) was walking in such circumstances when he sees a new scene:

Fa-idha alladhi ... yastasrikhuhu (28:18): "Suddenly he sees that the same man who had called him for help yesterday is calling him again today." This is the same person on whose behalf he had taken sides against the Egyptian the day before. This man is now quarrelling with another Egyptian and is calling out to Musa, "Save me from him." Perhaps his thought was that Musa would strike the other common enemy with a blow, as he had done before, and that this man too would fall in the same way.

But the thoughts of the one who had been killed had taken hold of Musa's mind, and he had already sought forgiveness from Allah for it. After being forgiven, he had made a covenant with Allah that from then on he would not side with any criminal, and the fear of the secret of the former deed being exposed was still alive. Now he became angry with the man who was calling for help. In anger he said to him that he was a great troublemaker.

Qala lahu Musa innaka lagawiyyun mubin (28:18): "Musa said, 'You are indeed a clearly misguided man.'" That is, you are such a person that you quarrel with everyone, and your quarrelling does not end; you have a dispute with everyone, which is of no benefit. In this way you will bring some great calamity upon the Children of Israel, and their position is such that they can neither bring about a revolution nor bear further oppression. At this time they are not in a position to launch any constructive movement. Therefore, there is no benefit in such partial clashes.

But even after this warning, Musa (peace be upon him) became angry with that Egyptian. Musa swooped upon him in the same way as he had done the previous day, and was about to finish him off in the same way as he had done yesterday. Here too it becomes apparent that the forceful temperament of Musa could not tolerate the oppression of the Egyptians. He became agitated because the oppression of the Egyptians had exceeded all limits. Therefore, his reaction against oppression and rebellion was natural, since these oppressions had been going on for a long time, and hatred against those people had been deeply and thoroughly filled in the hearts of the Children of Israel.

Falamma an arada an ... takuna min al-muslihin (28:19): "When he intended to strike the man who was an enemy of both of them, the man cried out, 'O Musa! Do you intend to kill me as you killed a person yesterday? You only want to be a tyrant in this land and do not want to be a reformer.'" Such words become common when a society has become corrupt, when oppression has become widespread, when high values have disappeared from society, when there is darkness everywhere. People begin to suffocate because of oppression. Circumstances, laws and customs all become corrupted, and human nature changes in such a way that people see oppression and no reaction arises within them. Injustice is being done to them, yet no spirit of resistance arises in their souls. Rather, people's nature becomes so corrupted that they begin to condemn the oppressed who defend their own oppression, and whoever stands with truth and raises his voice against tyranny is called a troublemaker and a terrorist, and is said to be trying to seize power by force. The words, "You killed a person yesterday and you want to live as a tyrant," were spoken by the Egyptian to Musa. This was because these Egyptians had seen only that the Israelites were being oppressed from every side, and they did not raise their heads. Thus it settled in their hearts that this is a high moral principle, that it is among the virtues of character, that it is a most civilised way of life, a superior moral conduct, and that the reform and welfare of society lies in no one lifting his head. When such people saw that, contrary to the response of the other oppressed, a person was defending himself, and was rebelling against the servile moral system that the rulers had established and according to which people were living, it was something unfamiliar to them, and fear would seize them. They would instead call the oppressed a tyrant and a violent man, accuse him of terrorism and immorality, and reproach and curse the oppressed. The curse and blame of such people rarely reached the oppressor; for the oppressed, there was no justification in their minds for self-defence, even if he had been driven to a dead end and had been forced to take a bold step.

The truth is that the Children of Israel were oppressed for a long period. Musa (peace be upon him), seeing this, became helpless; his patience overflowed. We see that first he defends an Israelite and then regrets it, but the pressure of circumstances is so severe that he is compelled to do the same act again, and he is about to carry it out. He resolves to seize the man who is an enemy of him and of his people.

For this reason Allah did not leave Musa to his deed; rather Allah trained him and accepted his supplication, because Allah is All-Knowing and All-Aware. He knows well how much endurance a human being has. When oppression becomes intense and all the doors of justice are closed, the oppressed is compelled to attack and is forced into some bold step. Therefore the Qur'an did not describe the act of killing on the part of Musa (peace be upon him) in a more frightening manner, unlike those societies which regard such an act as very frightening, whose nature and conscience have changed through bearing the oppressions of slavery. They do not understand that under the pressure of circumstances and in response to violence, people are compelled to such acts when their endurance comes to an end.

The manner in which the Qur'an mentions these two events conveys this very impression. The Qur'an neither gives a justification for these actions nor exaggerates their evil. However, the Qur'an called it a wrong to the self (zulm al-nafs) because Musa (peace be upon him) expressed tribal feelings at that point, while he was to be a future messenger and Allah Himself was training him under His own supervision. Or it is because Musa had begun a struggle against the oppression of Pharaoh before the appointed time, whereas Allah's will and plan was that the Children of Israel should receive complete collective deliverance, since no collective change is possible as a result of individual clashes, just as the Muslims in Makkah had been ordered to hold back their hands.

It appears that perhaps the news of the first killing had spread throughout Egypt. Suspicions had spread in government circles about Musa, since he had previously expressed displeasure at Pharaoh and his activities. It is also possible that the Israelites, with pride and joy, spread this secret along with Musa; especially within the circles of the Children of Israel it would have spread rapidly, and those outside would also have caught wind of it.

We prefer this view because in such circumstances, for Musa to kill one of Pharaoh's courtiers was a matter of joy and happiness for every Israelite. In this way the fire of their rage could be cooled. Such matters generally spread quickly from one to another, and sometimes pass from one circle to other circles, especially as it was well known about Musa that he kept expressing displeasure at this Pharaonic oppression and kept supporting the oppressed.

When Musa resolved to seize the second Egyptian and punish him, the man cried out and accused Musa of the killing of the first Egyptian, seeing that Musa was about to seize him, and perhaps the blow of the staff would prove fatal for him as well; so he cried out.

Aturidu an taqtulani kama qatalta nafsan bil-ams (28:19): "Do you intend to kill me as you killed a person yesterday?" As for the rest of the statement, in iin turid illa ... min al-muslihin (28:19): "You only want to be a tyrant in this land and do not want to be a reformer." From this it appears that at that time Musa (peace be upon him) had already started a movement of reform, and he was known as a reformer; therefore that man accuses him, saying that you are acting contrary to your own declared principles. You want to live in this land like a tyrant. Instead of reforming the situation, you want to kill people. Both the manner in which this man accuses Musa and the way he addresses him show that at this period Musa was not among Pharaoh's close associates and family members. Otherwise no Egyptian could have dared to make such an accusation against him, nor could his manner of address have been as it was.

Some commentators have said that these words belong to the Israelite on whose behalf Musa wished to seize the Egyptian, and not to the Egyptian himself, because Musa had rebuked the Israelite.

Innaka lagawiyyun mubin (28:18): "You are indeed a clearly misguided man." After this statement, when Musa advanced to seize the Egyptian, that Israelite assumed that perhaps the blow of the staff was about to fall upon him; so out of fear he made that accusation and disclosed the secret. These commentators adopted this opinion because, in Egypt, the secret of who the killer was had remained a secret.

However, it is more probable that this statement was made by the Egyptian. We have already explained that this secret had spread quietly throughout the whole city, and it is also possible that the Egyptian, through his shrewdness and wisdom, made the accusation that Musa could be the killer of the murdered man.

Apparently, when that man accused Musa of murder, Musa stopped from seizing him, and after escaping from here the man ran off and probably reached Pharaoh and said that the killer was actually Musa. Now there is a gap between the previous scene and the coming scene... The scene is that a man comes running from the city, outside the area of the royal court and residences, and warns Musa that discussions about him have begun at the highest level, and that it is better for him to save his life and leave Egypt.

[Translation of the given passage]

Then a man came running from the farthest part of the city and said, "O Musa, the chiefs are conferring about killing you. Leave this place; I am truly your well-wisher."

The chiefs of Pharaoh, his courtiers, his government officials and his inner circle came to know that Musa was behind the killing. Therefore they sensed that the danger had taken concrete form in the person of Musa, because this is an act whose nature is revolutionary and dangerous. It is the beginning of rebellion, and among its motives is the spirit of vengeance of the Children of Israel. Hence this is an extremely dangerous tendency, and severe measures are needed to prevent it. If this killing had been an ordinary incident, there would have been no need to consider it at the highest level. Killings among people happen every day, but this killing shook the entire system of government. They too began their measures, and the hand of divine power also began its work. From among the chiefs, a person who was sympathetic to Musa was used by the hand of divine power. This may well be the same man who was concealing his faith, and who is mentioned in verse 28 of Surah Ghafir. This man rose up and informed Musa about the counsels being held at the highest level. He came with seriousness, earnestness and haste, and informed Musa before the royal agents could take any action.

﴿Indeed, the chiefs are conferring about you, to kill you. So leave; indeed I am to you one of the sincere advisers.﴾ (28:20)

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 28, verse 21:

﴿فَخَرَجَ مِنْهَا خَائِفًا يَتَرَقَّبُ ۖ قَالَ رَبِّ نَجِّنِي مِنَ الْقَوْمِ الظَّالِمِينَ﴾ (21)

"So he left it, fearful and watchful. He said: 'My Lord, deliver me from the wrongdoing people.'"

Upon hearing this news, he went out fearful and frightened, and he prayed: "O my Lord, save me from the wrongdoers."

Prophet Musa (peace be upon him) left in fear and dread, alone and unaccompanied, and he had no provisions other than his trust in Allah. His attention was focused solely on Allah. He sought only Allah's help and guidance.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 28, verse 22:

﴿وَلَمَّا تَوَجَّهَ تِلْقَاءَ مَدْيَنَ قَالَ عَسَىٰ رَبِّي أَن يَهْدِيَنِي سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ﴾ (22)
"(When he left Egypt) and turned his face towards Madyan, he said: 'It may be that my Lord will guide me to the right path.'"

We see that Musa (peace be upon him) has been compelled to leave Egypt alone, and he is travelling alone towards Madyan through a barren desert without any provisions or equipment. The land of Madyan lies to the south of Syria and to the north of the Hijaz. It is a long journey, a distant one, for which Musa made no preparation. He left the city in a state of great fear, and the counsellor from among Pharaoh's chiefs had frightened him even more. Therefore he considered it wise to leave that place without a moment's delay. He did not doubt that counsellor's advice, nor did he hesitate in leaving. He did not delay in choosing a guide, nor did he seek out a travelling companion. Yet it is clear that his direction is towards Allah, and before Allah he has submitted completely. He seeks only Allah's guidance.

﴿عَسَىٰ رَبِّي أَن يَهْدِيَنِي سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ﴾ (28:22) "It may be that my Lord will guide me to the right path."

Once again we see that Musa has fallen into danger. After his childhood, he was living in great peace and comfort, residing very comfortably in the royal palace. But that same prince is now wandering the desert alone, with none of the world's provisions at his side. Pharaoh and his spies are in pursuit of him. He is being searched for everywhere. Today they wish to take revenge on him and snatch away the life that they could not take in his childhood. But the forces of divine power that saved him at that time are still with him today. Divine power will never allow him to be handed over to his enemies, for much work is yet to be done through him. Therefore he is travelling alone through the barren desert. Now he has reached a region where Pharaoh has no influence, and Pharaoh cannot harm him.

This long desert journey came to an end, and Musa (peace be upon him) arrived at a water-spring in Madyan. He was a weary traveller. At this spring he saw a scene that no noble and chivalrous man could bear to endure, and how then could Musa have borne it? He saw that male shepherds were bringing their animals forward and watering them, while two women were holding back their sheep away from the water. Yet the demand of sound human nature and chivalry is that the women be given the opportunity first, so that they may water their flocks and leave, and that men should give them room and cooperate with them. "Ladies First" is a natural principle.

Musa (peace be upon him) was a stranger in a foreign land, having left his own region, and he was also being pursued. He was exhausted and had come to this spring to rest. He saw that this scene was contrary to well-known moral principles. He stepped forward and asked these two women what the matter was.

﴿Qala ma khatbukuma﴾ (28:23) "What is your trouble?"

﴿Qalata la nasqi ... shaykhun kabir﴾ (28:23) "They said: We cannot water our animals until the shepherds take their animals away, and our father is a very old man." Thus they explained why they were holding back their animals and why they gave others the first opportunity. The reason was that they are women and weak, while the other shepherds are men and strong. And their father is old; he can neither graze the livestock nor confront those strong shepherds. The faith and innate nature of Musa (peace be upon him) was stirred. His sound nature awoke. He stepped forward and acted according to the principle, so that the helpless women might water first, as is the custom of noble and civilised people. Although he was a stranger in a foreign land, no one knew him, he had no supporter or helper here, he was exhausted, and he had reached here after cutting short a long journey. He had no one who knew him, no supporter or helper here, was exhausted, and had reached here after a long journey, and he also had no provisions for further travel. He was being pursued, and enemies were behind him, yet none of these circumstances could prevent him from showing chivalry and manliness on this occasion, nor from acting upon enjoining what is good, and from making people aware that the justice of nature requires that women be given the opportunity first.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 28, verse 24:

﴿So he watered their flocks for them﴾ (28: 24). "Hearing this, Musa watered their animals." Here the context shows that Musa (peace be upon him) was a person of refined upbringing and noble character. Physically too he was a strapping young man, at the sight of whom an ordinary person would be overawed, even though he had come tired from a long journey. The shepherds were affected more by his psychological superiority and moral conduct than by his physical strength, because people are more overawed by moral conduct than by physical power.

﴿Then he withdrew into the shade﴾ (28: 24). "Then he sat down in a shaded place." This shows that the weather was one of intense heat and scorching wind, and that Musa (peace be upon him) had to undertake this journey in such severe heat.

﴿And he said, "My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You would send down to me, in need."﴾ (28: 24). "And he said, 'O Lord, whatever good You bestow upon me, I am in need of it.'" At that moment he had taken physical refuge in the dense shade of the trees to rest his body, but along with this he was also seeking refuge in the shade of mercy of Allah, the Lord of Honour and the King who shows mercy and compassion. He had directed his soul and heart towards Allah. "O Allah, I am in need; I am alone, in a severe state. O Lord, I am without means; O Lord, I am greatly in need of Your grace, Your kindness and Your benevolence."

﴿Indeed, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾ (28: 24). We are still in this scene of Musa's (peace be upon him) supplication, when in the context there comes a most joyful glad tiding. It begins with the particle ﴿fa﴾ (then, immediately after), as if the Higher Realm had accepted Musa's prayer even before he lowered his hands, since he was making this supplication with the utmost humility.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 28, verse 25:

فجآء تہ احدھما ۔۔۔۔۔ اجر ما سقیت لنا۔

"(Not long after,) one of those two women came to him walking with modesty and said: 'My father invites you so that he may give you the reward for having watered our animals for us.'"

How generous is Allah's grace, and how close is Musa to Allah, that his call is heard so swiftly! The father of the two women, an elderly man of advanced years, invites Musa on the guidance of the Exalted Shaykh. This invitation is based on honour and respect, offering refuge and recompensing a kindness. The invitation is brought to him by one of the two maidens, and she comes "walking with modesty" (28:25). Her bearing is dignified, not wanton; she does not display her adornments but conceals them. There is neither feminine arrogance nor any display of allure. She comes and conveys the invitation on behalf of her father in very brief, comprehensive words. The Qur'an has recorded her words.

إن ربي ۔۔۔۔۔ سقيت لنا (28:25) "My father invites you so that he may give you the reward for having watered our animals for us." Within the bounds of modesty, with great clarity and in comprehensive words, she conveyed this message, without any affectation, hesitation or pause, and without any complication or stammering. Why is it so? Because this is the way of women of sound nature, chaste and straightforward character. A young woman of upright nature feels shy whenever she meets men; she is embarrassed to speak to them. Yet this girl, being self-assured, chaste and of sound nature, has no agitation in her speech. Otherwise, girls of base nature and character, on such occasions, adopt an attitude of coquetry, flirtation, and the creation of excitement. But this girl conveyed the desired message in very few words. She did not utter a single word beyond what was necessary.

The Qur'an also presents this very picture of the scene and adds nothing to it. Only one girl, on behalf of the aged shaykh, extends the invitation to him. Musa accepts, and the curtain falls. The next scene is their meeting. The Qur'an has not named this venerable shaykh. Some people have said that he was the nephew of the well-known Prophet Shu'ayb (peace be upon him), and that his name was Yathrun.

فلما جآءہ وقص ۔۔۔۔۔۔۔۔۔۔۔ من القوم الظلمين (25)

"When he came to him and related the whole story, he said: 'Do not fear; you have escaped from the wrongdoing people.'"

At that time, Musa's foremost need was a place of safety. He also needed a place where his food and drink would be arranged. But his need for a peaceful, secure and protected refuge was greater than his need for food and drink. This is why that serious, aged elderly man first said to him: "Do not fear." The first thing this man said to him was that he should be at ease and not be afraid, and after this assurance he said:

نجوت من القوم الظلمين (28:25) "You have escaped from the wrongdoing people." Their rule does not extend over Madyan. The people of Egypt cannot inflict any harm upon the inhabitants of Madyan.

Now the scene shifts to a very upright and chaste woman, and her voice is heard.

﴿One of the two women said: "O my father, hire him. Surely the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy."﴾ (28:26)

These two sisters had to tend sheep and goats, and when watering them they had to face the resistance of men, come into contact with men and be jostled by them, as every woman who does men's work is constantly confronted with such circumstances. These two sisters were continually distressed by this work. Their wish was to be confined to household affairs and to live the life of a chaste, modest woman who keeps to her home (zan-e-khana), and not to be compelled to mix with unrelated men at pastures and watering places. This is the natural conduct of chaste, pure-natured and upright women: they do not like to compete with men or to contend with them, and the lightness that arises within women from this kind of mixing and contention is something no upright-natured woman approves of.

Musa (peace be upon him) was young, a traveller and a stranger in a foreign land. Along with this he was strong and trustworthy. This woman had seen that all the shepherds had been awed by his strength and personality. They had immediately made way for Musa, and the animals of these two women had been able to drink. Although Musa was a stranger in a foreign land, and a stranger, even if he is a great man, is considered weak. And when this woman went to invite Musa, she had seen that he had a pure gaze and a pure tongue. So this woman advises her father: "Father, hire this man, so that he and his sister may be saved from the hardship of tending the sheep, and so that they are not made to do the work that men do." Musa is a robust man and trustworthy. For whoever proves trustworthy in the chastity of a maiden proves trustworthy in all matters. She also holds a perfectly clear view in this advice and speaks plainly; she has no fear that anyone will think ill of her, because the book of her heart is clear and her consciousness is pure, so she has no fear of being called to account. Thus she does not hesitate in her proposal, but makes it clearly and in the plainest words.

There is no need here to repeat the reports that the commentators have transmitted about Musa's (peace be upon him) strength, such as that the well from which the shepherds watered had a large stone placed over it, which twenty, forty or so people could lift. Yet the context of the Qur'an does not show that a stone lay over the well; rather, after the other shepherds had finished watering, these two women would water their flock. Musa drove the shepherds away and watered the animals of these women, or watered them alongside the other shepherds.

Nor is there any need to repeat the reports in which his honesty and trustworthiness are argued from the fact that he told the maiden: "Walk behind me and guide me from behind," lest his gaze fall upon this woman; or that Musa told the girl to walk behind him when she was walking ahead and the wind lifted her garments above her ankles. These are mere embellishments, and through them an attempt is made to remove doubts that have no existence at all. Musa himself was chaste in his gaze and had pure sentiments, and this woman too was chaste. Where chastity and trustworthiness exist, there is no need for embellishments to prove them, especially at the time of a meeting between a man and a woman, because chastity is a firm disposition that forms part of one's character without any affectation or pretence.

The old man accepted his daughter's proposal. He perceived that desire and confidence existed in both the girl and Musa, and that a natural inclination was present, and that together they could lay the foundation of a righteous family. When a young man combines strength and chastity, by nature every upright-natured maiden agrees to make such a person her life partner, one who is himself chaste and righteous. Therefore the old man made Musa an offer: that he could give him one of his daughters in marriage, on condition that Musa serve him for eight years and graze his livestock; and if Musa chose to serve for ten years as a favour, it would be an act of kindness on Musa's part.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 28, verse 27:

He said, "I wish to marry one of these two daughters of mine to you, on condition that you serve me for eight years; and if you complete ten, it is up to you. I do not wish to impose hardship upon you. You will find me, God willing, among the righteous." (28:27)

In such simplicity and without any formality, this man himself made the offer to give one of his two daughters in marriage to Musa (peace be upon him). Perhaps it was the same girl who had made the suggestion, and there was a mutual inclination of hearts between her and Musa (peace be upon him). The man spoke without reserve and made the offer directly and plainly, because the offer was for a marriage contract. Therefore there was no need to feel any shyness in it, since the offer was made so that a new family might come into being. This man did not adopt the pretence of speaking through allusion and indirect hints. Such affectations and artificialities exist in those societies in which a departure from human nature has occurred, and such societies fall prey to extremely false, filthy customs and formalities. Because of these formalities, a father or guardian never makes a clear offer to give a girl in marriage to someone, although in his heart he likes many people. He understands well that a certain match would be very beneficial for his daughter, sister or relative, yet people wait for some proposal from the husband, his representative or his guardian; generally it is considered that an offer from the woman's side is not appropriate.

But one of the contradictions of such unnatural and rotten societies is that young men and women maintain free mixing with one another, they engage in free conversation, they tolerate free intermingling and mutual disclosure, yet a proposal of nikah and marriage is considered objectionable. When a proposal of marriage is made, artificial veiling and concealment begin at that very time, and the boy and girl stop speaking with one another; indeed, a barrier begins. In short, in a proposal of marriage there is no natural openness, although it should have simplicity and frankness.

In the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, fathers would plainly offer their daughters in marriage, and even women would offer themselves. Women would offer themselves in marriage to the Prophet ﷺ, or would make a direct offer to those men who were interested in marrying them. This matter would be settled with great simplicity, openly, without formality and with frankness. There were no particular etiquettes or formalities for it, and such an offer did not diminish anyone's honour or nobility. When Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) offered his daughter Hafsah to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him), he remained silent. Then he offered her to Uthman, and he expressed his apology. When he informed the Messenger ﷺ that he had done so, the Messenger ﷺ was very pleased and said that it might be that Allah would give her a match better than both of them. After this, the Messenger ﷺ himself entered into marriage with her. Another woman offered herself to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he apologised. Then that woman gave the right of her nikah to the Messenger ﷺ. The Messenger ﷺ married her to a man who had two surahs of the Qur'an, and the Messenger ﷺ married that woman to him and made those two surahs her mahr.

This was the simplicity with which families were being formed in the Islamic society, and in this way an Islamic society was coming into being. In this matter there was no allusion, no indirection, no formality, no artifice and no crookedness among them. The old man of Madyan also did the same. He himself made this offer to Musa (peace be upon him), and also promised that during this period he would not impose any hardship on him and would not burden him beyond his capacity. He hoped that you would play the role of a righteous young man, and that you would deal with our affairs with fairness. These are extremely beautiful and simple manners. They neither raise themselves to the heavens, nor recount tales of their own purity and chastity, nor praise Musa (peace be upon him) with flattery. Rather, they only hope for good, and they entrust all matters to the will of Allah.

Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) also accepted this proposal with the same simplicity, sincerity and openness, and made Allah his witness in it, for there was no one there to witness it besides Allah.

Qala dhalika bayni wa baynak ... ma naqoolu wakeel (28)

When two parties enter into an agreement, there should be no ambiguity in it, nor should the matter be left vague. At the time of the contract, the terms should not be concealed; rather, everything should be stated openly. At the time of a contract, one should not feel shy in clarifying any point. This is why Hazrat Musa accepted the offer and entered into the marriage. Regarding the conditional proposal made by that old man, Hazrat Musa clarifies that he will fulfil whichever of the two terms he (the father-in-law) wishes.

Ayyamal ajalayni qadaytu fala udwana alayya (28:28): "Whichever of the two terms I fulfil, there shall be no transgression against me afterwards." Whether I stay eight years or complete ten years, there will be no excess in the obligations of the work. That is, the addition of two years beyond eight is optional, and Allah is witness to this agreement of ours, because He sees, and Allah is a witness to both parties entering into a contract, and He is a sufficient witness.

Hazrat Musa gave this statement in complete accordance with his nature. He was of an extremely straightforward and open disposition. The clarification he gave about completing ten years, stating clearly that it was optional, was because it is the duty of the parties to a contract to speak plainly. Yet his intention was to act upon the longer of the two terms. It is related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) completed the longer and fuller term (Bukhari).

Thus Hazrat Musa (peace be upon him) remained in his father-in-law's house with great honour and respect. He was safe and protected from Pharaoh and his plots. Everything that was happening was occurring in accordance with Allah's perfect wisdom. Now, leave aside how those ten years passed; they have no importance in our narrative. The Qur'an has cut away the scenes of them and remains silent. The curtain falls.

In short, those ten years passed, upon which the parties had concluded the agreement. Nothing is mentioned about them in this surah.

Now, in the next scene, Hazrat Musa is seen, having completed the ten-year term, travelling towards Egypt. He is leaving Madyan and returning to Egypt. He is returning along the same paths by which he had come alone, fearful and frightened, but now the atmosphere of his return is not like the atmosphere of his flight. He was returning, but the experiences he was about to encounter along the way were not even in his imagination, namely that the Lord, the Exalted, would call out to him. Now he would become Musa, the one spoken to by Allah, and the mission would be entrusted to him, for which Allah had kept him under His watchful eye, and nurtured and trained him. And what was this mission? To raise the word of truth before Pharaoh, the tyrant, and his chiefs; and the word was this: free the Children of Israel so that they may worship their Lord as they wish and associate none with Him, and that they liberate the land which Allah had promised them, and that Hazrat Musa be an adversary to Pharaoh, Haman and their followers and a source of distress to them, so that the end of both of them would come at the hands of Hazrat Musa, for this was the true promise of Allah.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (*Fi Zilal al-Quran*, Urdu translation) on Surah 28, verses 29–35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So when Musa had fulfilled the term and set out with his family, he saw a fire on the side of the mount. He said to his family, "Wait, I have seen a fire. Perhaps I can bring you news from it, or a burning brand so that you may warm yourselves."﴾ (28:29)

Before we discuss in detail these two scenes of this section, we should reflect on what measures and steps Allah took concerning Musa (peace be upon him) during these ten years, and what wisdom lay in this journey and in this coming and going.

The hand of divine power willed that Musa (peace be upon him) should advance step by step. From the time when he was a suckling infant until his present position, the dealings of divine power with him were these. He was cast into the river so that Pharaoh's people would pick him up. Seeing him, Pharaoh's wife became captivated by him, or was made to become captivated, so that he would be raised in the very palace of the king, growing up in the house of the enemy. Then he entered the city at a time of people's heedlessness, and a man died at his hands. Then a man from among Pharaoh's courtiers was sent to him, saying, "Leave, for the plans for your killing are being made." This divine support remained with him through the desert journey from Egypt to Madyan, while he had no provisions or equipment. Then at the well of Madyan he was brought into contact with the daughters of the Shaykh, and a ten-year agreement was concluded between him and that excellent mentor and elderly man. And when he returned from there, the great mission was entrusted to him at Tur.

Before the call to entrust the mission, Allah's great favour and kindness continued upon him. He was instructed continually, and all the heavenly forces kept supporting him. He was subjected to various experiences of life: the experience of kindness, love and guidance; the experience of taking an extreme step under the pressure of circumstances; the experience of feeling remorse, of exercising caution, and of seeking forgiveness for a mistake; the experience of fear, pursuit and anxiety; the experience of solitude, travel, hunger and poverty; and the experience of serving others and even tending sheep. And amid these great experiences were smaller experiences of everyday life, various inner feelings, different kinds of thoughts and anxieties, new discoveries and information. Along with all this, it should also be remembered that Allah had endowed him with knowledge and wisdom as soon as he reached youth. (These experiences were made to undergo while he was in the position of a prince, taken out from that position.)

The truth is that the office of prophethood (*risalah*) is a duty and a great responsibility with many aspects, and manifold obligations fall upon the Prophet and the Messenger. Therefore it is extremely necessary for a Prophet to comprehend knowledge and excellence, wisdom and understanding, various experiences of life, and the practical lives of different people. And this practical experience is distinct from that theoretical knowledge and wisdom and from the divine revelation that is given to every Prophet, so that the conscience of the Prophet becomes pure and clean, and guidance is firmly placed in the heart of the Prophet.

From the history of the Messengers it becomes known that, apart from the missions entrusted to all the Prophets, the responsibilities of Musa (peace be upon him) were very heavy and difficult. He had to go before a rebellious and tyrannical ruler like Pharaoh. He was the greatest and wealthiest king of his era, the master of an ancient royal line. His government was extremely stable, and Egypt was then advanced in terms of civilisation and culture. He had reduced all the oppressed nations to slavery, and he held a high station on the earth.

Then Musa (peace be upon him) was sent for the liberation and migration of a people in whose hearts and minds slavery had taken root. They had become accustomed to a life of servitude, and their conscience had completely changed. They had in practice remained slaves for a very long time. The truth is that slavery corrupts human nature. Rot and stench arise within it, and such a people lose all sense of the filth, stench and rot. They cannot bear goodness, virtue, beauty and excellence. To raise such a corrupted people is a meaningful undertaking.

He was sent to a people who had once held the Islamic ideology from ancient times, but in whom a doctrinal deviation had arisen. In their hearts and minds that original, true form no longer existed. This people were neither upholding the old Islamic belief and Shariah, nor accepting the new belief properly. To reform such people is an extremely difficult task. To correct the crookedness within them, to straighten their deviation, and to remove the deep layers of superstition from their original beliefs were the most difficult aspects of this endeavour.

In brief, Musa was to build an entirely new community (*ummah*). From the very beginning, for the first time, he had to make the Children of Israel a distinct people, a people possessing a particular system, and a community bearing a particular messengership. And it is evident that building a people and a community is an extremely difficult task. This is why the Quran has repeated the story of Musa (peace be upon him) again and again. Because in the building of a new community upon the foundation of an ideology, the life of Musa (peace be upon him) was a specific model. In the path of such a great work there are internal and external difficulties. In such all-embracing calls, deviation also keeps arising. It also takes on specific forms, and it must pass through many experiences. And obstacles also come along the way.

The question is: why was Musa (peace be upon him) made to pass through the Bedouin-like life of Madyan? The answer is that this was so that he might also learn the ups and downs of the laborious life of common people and gain direct experience of it.

The life of royal palaces has a particular atmosphere, particular etiquettes and protocols. Even if someone is of sound nature, pure disposition, and possessed of knowledge and excellence, the shadow of palace life inevitably falls upon him, and some of its effects remain. As far as prophethood is concerned, a Messenger deals with the rich as well as with the poor. In the community there are wealthy people and there are poor people. Among them there are clean people and there are people who are dirty and unkempt, cultured people and savage people. There are people of pure nature and people of corrupt nature, good people and bad people, strong people and weak people, patient people and people who lament and wail. In short, the community contains every kind of person, and the Prophet has to reform them all. The poor have their own habits in eating, drinking, walking, and dress. They understand matters according to their own minds. They have a particular conception of life; their speech, their movements and gestures, their discourse and the manner of their awareness are of a distinct style. These common habits weigh very heavily upon those who were raised in palaces. People of lofty palaces do not even have the patience to look at the common manners of these people, let alone tolerate them and treat them. Although the hearts of these common people are full of goodness, and they are receptive to reform, because their outward manners and habits do not suit the one of the lofty palace.

A Messenger sometimes has to face hardships, solitude and poverty. But those who are accustomed to living in great palaces, however fervent their spirit of sacrifice may be, cannot endure poverty, deprivation and the hardships of practical life for a very long time, because they have become accustomed within palaces to luxury, abundance and ease.

Therefore, the will of Allah required that Musa (peace be upon him) be brought down a little from that high standard of palace life to the level of common life. He was to be placed within the society of shepherds, and after flight from fear, pursuit and the dread of being seized, he was to be accustomed to living the life of a shepherd, where he would receive only food and shelter. This was so that the arrogance that princes have toward poverty and the poor might be removed, and the aversion that princes harbour toward the habits, morals, roughness and simplicity of shepherds might be removed. So that Musa, the prince, would not consider himself exalted and distant from their ignorance, poverty, wretchedness and general ways. And so that he would be cast into the deep seas of common life, whereas previously he had been swimming within a limited stream of human life, so that he might be well prepared for the life of calling to the faith that lay ahead.

When the personality of Musa (peace be upon him) had completed these experiences and he became thoroughly familiar with the ups and downs of common life, and these experiences had come to him while living in another land as a stranger far from home, then the hand of divine power sent him back to the place of his birth, where his family and his people lived, and where he was to discharge the most difficult duty of prophethood. Now he is treading that same path. He had fled from it and had been running away completely alone. The question is: why did he come upon this same road and return? In fact, this was a kind of military exercise, intended to acquaint him with the ups and downs and the paths and passes of that road. Because the divine power had decided that soon Musa would lead his people along this very road into Sinai. This was in fact the training of every vanguard and leader, so that Musa would not need any other guide than himself, not even one to show him the way. For his people had fallen into a state in which they needed guidance in every matter, great and small, since humiliation, slavery and subjugation had utterly corrupted them. No reflection and no thought remained within them.

Now it has become clear how the divine power was training Musa (peace be upon him) under its own watchful eye, and how he was given excellent training for the performance of his prophetic duty. Now let us see how Musa undertook the journey of return.

﴿So when Musa had fulfilled the term and set out with his family, he saw a fire on the side of the mount. He said to his family, "Wait, I have seen a fire. Perhaps I can bring you news from it, or a burning brand so that you may warm yourselves."﴾ (28:29)

Here there is an important question: what was the thinking that moved Musa (peace be upon him) to return to Egypt? He had completed the period of his service in Madyan. Now he is returning to Egypt, although he had left Egypt in a state of great fear. He was in dread of pursuit. He was returning as though he had forgotten the danger that still awaited him in Egypt. There he had killed a man, and Pharaoh, who was still alive, was consulting with his chiefs about killing him.

The truth is that all this was taking place according to the plan of the higher realm. This time, perhaps the natural inclination toward family, people and homeland compelled him to return, and the dangers that had led him to flee alone from here had vanished from his heart. And this divine power was doing so in order that he might be made ready for the mission and office for which Allah had created him from the first day.

Whatever the reason, Musa is returning. His family is with him. It is night, and the darkness is intense. The caravan has lost its way. It is the winter season. He is going to fetch fire from there, since he saw a fire. The purpose is that whoever is beside the fire will either show him the way, or else he will bring back a brand to warm themselves. This is the first scene of this part.

The second scene is most unexpected.

﴿And when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree: "O Musa, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ (28:30)

Musa sees that there is a fire, and that in the valley of Tur it is on his right. This place is extraordinarily blessed, and on this very day this valley is being made blessed. The whole of creation is silent for a moment, and within it the voice of the higher realm and of the Lord of Majesty is resounding. Apparently the voice is coming to his ears from a blessed tree, and perhaps it is the only tree in that region.

﴿O Musa, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ (28:30) Musa heard this voice directly. He stood alone in that deep and silent valley, in a night extremely dark and still. This voice... the whole universe was also hearing it from every side; it was resounding in the distances and heights of the earth and the heavens. Musa perceived this voice. By what means he perceived it, and in what manner he heard it, we do not know. What is certain is that the being of Musa, his surroundings and the entire universe were resounding with it and filled with it. Musa (peace be upon him) perceived the voice of the Lord of the universe and was able to bear it, because he had been prepared for it. The universe recorded this voice. The place where Musa perceived it became blessed. That place now became honoured, and Musa was now standing in a most blessed and honoured place, and this voice has not yet ended; the dialogue is continuing.

﴿Throw down your staff.﴾ (28:31) Musa, obeying the command of the Lord, immediately threw down his staff. And behold, it is no longer the staff that had been with him for a long time, which he knew certainly to be a staff. It is no longer a staff; it has become a serpent crawling on the ground, moving very swiftly here and there, and it is twisting in the manner in which small serpents twist, although it appears to be a very large serpent.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 28, verse 29–35 (part 2 of 2):

﴿فَلَمَّا رَآهَا تَهْتَزُّ كَأَنَّهَا جَانٌّ وَلَّىٰ مُدْبِرًا وَلَمْ يُعَقِّبْ﴾ (28: 31) "When he saw it moving like a snake, he turned and fled without looking back." This was an extremely unexpected situation; he was not mentally prepared for it, and moreover his temperament was receptive, so every situation affected him quickly. He fled in such a way that he did not even look back to see whether the snake was advancing toward him or not, so that he might find out that this was a strange miracle and reflect upon it. Those who are quickly affected behave in this manner. The divine call continues:

﴿يَا مُوسَىٰ أَقْبِلْ وَلَا تَخَفْ إِنَّكَ مِنَ الْآمِنِينَ﴾ (28: 31) "O Musa, come back and do not fear; you are perfectly safe." Experiences of fear and security were not new to Musa (peace be upon him). His life, through its various stages, consisted of cycles of fear and security. Fear and security were the seasons of his whole life, from beginning to end. For Musa (peace be upon him) to be affected in this way was also based on the wisdom of God, and was desired and intended. It was thus destined in his life, because the ups and downs, the agitation and the turmoil in the life of Musa were deliberately created in contrast to the static, imitative and stagnant life of the Children of Israel. This was the decree of nature, and it was based on the profound wisdom and planning of nature.

﴿أَقْبِلْ وَلَا تَخَفْ إِنَّكَ مِنَ الْآمِنِينَ﴾ (28: 31) "Come back, and do not fear; you are safe." How could one not be safe whom the hand of power is advancing and whom Allah Himself is watching over? The dialogue is still continuing.

﴿اسْلُكْ يَدَكَ فِي جَيْبِكَ تَخْرُجْ بَيْضَاءَ مِنْ غَيْرِ سُوءٍ﴾ (28: 32) "Put your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without any harm." Musa obeyed the command and put his hand into his bosom and drew it out. At that moment this was a second unexpected sight for him: the hand was white and shining, and without any disease, although previously it had been wheat-coloured. The indication in the whiteness of the hand was that truth and reality are clear, bright and luminous like the daylight.

Now the emotional and easily affected personality of Musa showed its effect. He was frightened on seeing these scenes, these unexpected sights,
and began to tremble. Once again divine guidance comes directly. The command is given that he should press his hands and arms to himself; in this way the beating of his heart will decrease and he will attain complete tranquillity.

﴿وَاضْمُمْ إِلَيْكَ جَنَاحَكَ مِنَ الرَّهْبِ﴾ (28: 32) "And press your arm to your side to banish fear." Thus his hands are his wings, which he joins to his chest, just as a bird, once it is at rest, folds its wings to its body. When a bird flutters its wings, its state resembles that of agitation. The Qur'an here paints such a picture of this meaning:

Now Musa (peace be upon him) has received guidance from the Lord and has been shown the observations that were made to him. He has already seen these two signs and miracles himself. First he himself became frightened and his heart began to pound; then he was given reassurance. Now the real mission is entrusted to him, for which he has been trained from the beginning, from the time of his birth.

﴿فَذَانِكَ بُرْهَانَانِ مِنْ رَبِّكَ إِلَىٰ فِرْعَوْنَ وَمَلَئِهِ ۚ إِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا قَوْمًا فَاسِقِينَ﴾ (28: 32) "These are two clear proofs from your Lord to be presented before Pharaoh and his chiefs; they are a people who are rebellious."

This message was, as it were, for Pharaoh and his chieftains. And this was the fulfilment of the promise made to the mother of Musa (peace be upon him): "We shall return him to you and make him one of the messengers." It was a firm promise, and many years had passed since it was settled. But it was Allah's promise, and Allah does not break His promise; He is the Speaker of the most truthful word.

Now Musa (peace be upon him) recalls that he had killed a man of theirs, and that he had left them at a time when there was a danger of arrest, and that he had fled because they had begun consulting about killing him. The dialogue of Musa with the Lord was in progress, and this was a great honour bestowed upon him. Then he was granted the honour of two great miracles. And then He trained him under His own supervision. Therefore he expressed, concerning his mission, a fear about a practical difficulty: lest those people kill him at once and the chain of the call be cut off.

﴿قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي قَتَلْتُ مِنْهُمْ نَفْسًا فَأَخَافُ أَن يَقْتُلُونِ﴾ (28: 33) "He said: My Lord, I have killed a man of theirs, and I fear that they will kill me." Musa (peace be upon him) was not making an excuse for declining the office of prophethood, nor did he intend to back away, turn aside or disobey. Rather, he sought assurance and wished for the reassurance that the call should continue. And if he were killed, as is feared, the whole process would end from its very beginning. This was also a prudent point on his part, although he was strong and trustworthy and was not one who feared.

﴿وَأَخِي هَارُونُ هُوَ أَفْصَحُ مِنِّي لِسَانًا فَأَرْسِلْهُ مَعِيَ رِدْءًا يُصَدِّقُنِي ۖ إِنِّي أَخَافُ أَن يُكَذِّبُونِ﴾ (28: 34) "And my brother Harun is more eloquent in speech than I; so send him with me as a helper to confirm me. I fear that they will call me a liar." Harun is more eloquent and articulate than me and can present the call well; send him to me as a supporter, so that he may confirm my claim to prophethood, and if they kill me, he will be my successor. Thus Musa (peace be upon him) is given assurance and his request is accepted.

﴿قَالَ سَنَشُدُّ عَضُدَكَ بِأَخِيكَ وَنَجْعَلُ لَكُمَا سُلْطَانًا فَلَا يَصِلُونَ إِلَيْكُمَا ۚ بِآيَاتِنَا ۚ أَنتُمَا وَمَنِ اتَّبَعَكُمَا الْغَالِبُونَ﴾ (28: 35) "He said: We will strengthen your arm through your brother, and We will give you both authority, so that they will not reach you. By Our signs, you and those who follow you will be the victors." In whatever events take place, the miraculous powers of divine power appear more clearly working with Musa, so that behind the success and victory of Musa one sees not only the known causes, but the colour of the will of the higher realm predominates; so that, alongside material causes, the will of the heavenly powers also clearly takes on importance in people's thinking. People should attain faith in Allah, trust in Allah, and leave the outcomes to Allah.

This beautiful and great scene comes to an end, the distances of time and place are folded up, and Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) are now in the court of Pharaoh, bearing the clear signs of Allah. Now guidance and misguidance stand face to face. A harsh dialogue between them has begun. And in this world the contest between truth and falsehood is decided in such a way that falsehood, with its hosts and its armies, is drowned. And in the Hereafter it will certainly be deserving of curse.

Because the divine power had decided that soon Musa would lead his people along this very road into Sinai. This was in fact the training of every vanguard and leader, so that Musa would not need any other guide than himself, not even one to show him the way. For his people had fallen into a state in which they needed guidance in every matter, great and small, since humiliation, slavery and subjugation had utterly corrupted them. No reflection and no thought remained within them.

Now it has become clear how the divine power was training Musa (peace be upon him) under its own watchful eye, and how he was given excellent training for the performance of his prophetic duty. Now let us see how Musa undertook the journey of return.

﴿So when Musa had fulfilled the term and set out with his family, he saw a fire on the side of the mount. He said to his family, "Wait, I have seen a fire. Perhaps I can bring you news from it, or a burning brand so that you may warm yourselves."﴾ (28:29)

Here there is an important question: what was the thinking that moved Musa (peace be upon him) to return to Egypt? He had completed the period of his service in Madyan. Now he is returning to Egypt, although he had left Egypt in a state of great fear. He was in dread of pursuit. He was returning as though he had forgotten the danger that still awaited him in Egypt. There he had killed a man, and Pharaoh, who was still alive, was consulting with his chiefs about killing him.

The truth is that all this was taking place according to the plan of the higher realm. This time, perhaps the natural inclination toward family, people and homeland compelled him to return, and the dangers that had led him to flee alone from here had vanished from his heart. And this divine power was doing so in order that he might be made ready for the mission and office for which Allah had created him from the first day.

Whatever the reason, Musa is returning. His family is with him. It is night, and the darkness is intense. The caravan has lost its way. It is the winter season. He is going to fetch fire from there, since he saw a fire. The purpose is that whoever is beside the fire will either show him the way, or else he will bring back a brand to warm themselves. This is the first scene of this part.

The second scene is most unexpected.

﴿And when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree: "O Musa, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds."﴾ (28:30)

Musa sees that there is a fire, and that in the valley of Tur it is on his right. This place is extraordinarily blessed, and on this very day this valley is being made blessed. The whole of creation is silent for a moment, and within it the voice of the higher realm and of the Lord of Majesty is resounding. Apparently the voice is coming to his ears from a blessed tree, and perhaps it is the only tree in that region.

﴿O Musa, indeed I am Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ (28:30) Musa heard this voice directly. He stood alone in that deep and silent valley, in a night extremely dark and still. This voice... the whole universe was also hearing it from every side; it was resounding in the distances and heights of the earth and the heavens. Musa perceived this voice. By what means he perceived it, and in what manner he heard it, we do not know. What is certain is that the being of Musa, his surroundings and the entire universe were resounding with it and filled with it. Musa (peace be upon him) perceived the voice of the Lord of the universe and was able to bear it, because he had been prepared for it. The universe recorded this voice. The place where Musa perceived it became blessed. That place now became honoured, and Musa was now standing in a most blessed and honoured place, and this voice has not yet ended; the dialogue is continuing.

﴿Throw down your staff.﴾ (28:31) Musa, obeying the command of the Lord, immediately threw down his staff. And behold, it is no longer the staff that had been with him for a long time, which he knew certainly to be a staff. It is no longer a staff; it has become a serpent crawling on the ground, moving very swiftly here and there, and it is twisting in the manner in which small serpents twist, although it appears to be a very large serpent.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran (Urdu translation)) on surah 28, verse 29–35 (part 2 of 2):

﴿فَلَمَّا رَآهَا تَهْتَزُّ كَأَنَّهَا جَانٌّ وَلَّىٰ مُدْبِرًا وَلَمْ يُعَقِّبْ﴾ (28: 31) "When he saw it moving like a snake, he turned and fled without looking back." This was an extremely unexpected situation; he was not mentally prepared for it, and moreover his temperament was receptive, so every situation affected him quickly. He fled in such a way that he did not even look back to see whether the snake was advancing toward him or not, so that he might find out that this was a strange miracle and reflect upon it. Those who are quickly affected behave in this manner. The divine call continues:

﴿يَا مُوسَىٰ أَقْبِلْ وَلَا تَخَفْ إِنَّكَ مِنَ الْآمِنِينَ﴾ (28: 31) "O Musa, come back and do not fear; you are perfectly safe." Experiences of fear and security were not new to Musa (peace be upon him). His life, through its various stages, consisted of cycles of fear and security. Fear and security were the seasons of his whole life, from beginning to end. For Musa (peace be upon him) to be affected in this way was also based on the wisdom of God, and was desired and intended. It was thus destined in his life, because the ups and downs, the agitation and the turmoil in the life of Musa were deliberately created in contrast to the static, imitative and stagnant life of the Children of Israel. This was the decree of nature, and it was based on the profound wisdom and planning of nature.

﴿أَقْبِلْ وَلَا تَخَفْ إِنَّكَ مِنَ الْآمِنِينَ﴾ (28: 31) "Come back, and do not fear; you are safe." How could one not be safe whom the hand of power is advancing and whom Allah Himself is watching over? The dialogue is still continuing.

﴿اسْلُكْ يَدَكَ فِي جَيْبِكَ تَخْرُجْ بَيْضَاءَ مِنْ غَيْرِ سُوءٍ﴾ (28: 32) "Put your hand into your bosom; it will come out white without any harm." Musa obeyed the command and put his hand into his bosom and drew it out. At that moment this was a second unexpected sight for him: the hand was white and shining, and without any disease, although previously it had been wheat-coloured. The indication in the whiteness of the hand was that truth and reality are clear, bright and luminous like the daylight.

Now the emotional and easily affected personality of Musa showed its effect. He was frightened on seeing these scenes, these unexpected sights,
and began to tremble. Once again divine guidance comes directly. The command is given that he should press his hands and arms to himself; in this way the beating of his heart will decrease and he will attain complete tranquillity.

﴿وَاضْمُمْ إِلَيْكَ جَنَاحَكَ مِنَ الرَّهْبِ﴾ (28: 32) "And press your arm to your side to banish fear." Thus his hands are his wings, which he joins to his chest, just as a bird, once it is at rest, folds its wings to its body. When a bird flutters its wings, its state resembles that of agitation. The Qur'an here paints such a picture of this meaning:

Now Musa (peace be upon him) has received guidance from the Lord and has been shown the observations that were made to him. He has already seen these two signs and miracles himself. First he himself became frightened and his heart began to pound; then he was given reassurance. Now the real mission is entrusted to him, for which he has been trained from the beginning, from the time of his birth.

﴿فَذَانِكَ بُرْهَانَانِ مِنْ رَبِّكَ إِلَىٰ فِرْعَوْنَ وَمَلَئِهِ ۚ إِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا قَوْمًا فَاسِقِينَ﴾ (28: 32) "These are two clear proofs from your Lord to be presented before Pharaoh and his chiefs; they are a people who are rebellious."

This message was, as it were, for Pharaoh and his chieftains. And this was the fulfilment of the promise made to the mother of Musa (peace be upon him): "We shall return him to you and make him one of the messengers." It was a firm promise, and many years had passed since it was settled. But it was Allah's promise, and Allah does not break His promise; He is the Speaker of the most truthful word.

Now Musa (peace be upon him) recalls that he had killed a man of theirs, and that he had left them at a time when there was a danger of arrest, and that he had fled because they had begun consulting about killing him. The dialogue of Musa with the Lord was in progress, and this was a great honour bestowed upon him. Then he was granted the honour of two great miracles. And then He trained him under His own supervision. Therefore he expressed, concerning his mission, a fear about a practical difficulty: lest those people kill him at once and the chain of the call be cut off.

﴿قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي قَتَلْتُ مِنْهُمْ نَفْسًا فَأَخَافُ أَن يَقْتُلُونِ﴾ (28: 33) "He said: My Lord, I have killed a man of theirs, and I fear that they will kill me." Musa (peace be upon him) was not making an excuse for declining the office of prophethood, nor did he intend to back away, turn aside or disobey. Rather, he sought assurance and wished for the reassurance that the call should continue. And if he were killed, as is feared, the whole process would end from its very beginning. This was also a prudent point on his part, although he was strong and trustworthy and was not one who feared.

﴿وَأَخِي هَارُونُ هُوَ أَفْصَحُ مِنِّي لِسَانًا فَأَرْسِلْهُ مَعِيَ رِدْءًا يُصَدِّقُنِي ۖ إِنِّي أَخَافُ أَن يُكَذِّبُونِ﴾ (28: 34) "And my brother Harun is more eloquent in speech than I; so send him with me as a helper to confirm me. I fear that they will call me a liar." Harun is more eloquent and articulate than me and can present the call well; send him to me as a supporter, so that he may confirm my claim to prophethood, and if they kill me, he will be my successor. Thus Musa (peace be upon him) is given assurance and his request is accepted.

﴿قَالَ سَنَشُدُّ عَضُدَكَ بِأَخِيكَ وَنَجْعَلُ لَكُمَا سُلْطَانًا فَلَا يَصِلُونَ إِلَيْكُمَا ۚ بِآيَاتِنَا ۚ أَنتُمَا وَمَنِ اتَّبَعَكُمَا الْغَالِبُونَ﴾ (28: 35) "He said: We will strengthen your arm through your brother, and We will give you both authority, so that they will not reach you. By Our signs, you and those who follow you will be the victors." In whatever events take place, the miraculous powers of divine power appear more clearly working with Musa, so that behind the success and victory of Musa one sees not only the known causes, but the colour of the will of the higher realm predominates; so that, alongside material causes, the will of the heavenly powers also clearly takes on importance in people's thinking. People should attain faith in Allah, trust in Allah, and leave the outcomes to Allah.

This beautiful and great scene comes to an end, the distances of time and place are folded up, and Musa and Harun (peace be upon them) are now in the court of Pharaoh, bearing the clear signs of Allah. Now guidance and misguidance stand face to face. A harsh dialogue between them has begun. And in this world the contest between truth and falsehood is decided in such a way that falsehood, with its hosts and its armies, is drowned. And in the Hereafter it will certainly be deserving of curse.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (*Fi Zilal al-Quran*, Urdu translation) on Surah 28, verses 29–35 (part 1 of 2):

﴿So when Musa had fulfilled the term and set out with his family, he saw a fire on the side of the mount. He said to his family, "Wait, I have seen a fire. Perhaps I can bring you news from it, or a burning brand so that you may warm yourselves."﴾ (28:29)

Before we discuss in detail these two scenes of this section, we should reflect on what measures and steps Allah took concerning Musa (peace be upon him) during these ten years, and what wisdom lay in this journey and in this coming and going.

The hand of divine power willed that Musa (peace be upon him) should advance step by step. From the time when he was a suckling infant until his present position, the dealings of divine power with him were these. He was cast into the river so that Pharaoh's people would pick him up. Seeing him, Pharaoh's wife became captivated by him, or was made to become captivated, so that he would be raised in the very palace of the king, growing up in the house of the enemy. Then he entered the city at a time of people's heedlessness, and a man died at his hands. Then a man from among Pharaoh's courtiers was sent to him, saying, "Leave, for the plans for your killing are being made." This divine support remained with him through the desert journey from Egypt to Madyan, while he had no provisions or equipment. Then at the well of Madyan he was brought into contact with the daughters of the Shaykh, and a ten-year agreement was concluded between him and that excellent mentor and elderly man. And when he returned from there, the great mission was entrusted to him at Tur.

Before the call to entrust the mission, Allah's great favour and kindness continued upon him. He was instructed continually, and all the heavenly forces kept supporting him. He was subjected to various experiences of life: the experience of kindness, love and guidance; the experience of taking an extreme step under the pressure of circumstances; the experience of feeling remorse, of exercising caution, and of seeking forgiveness for a mistake; the experience of fear, pursuit and anxiety; the experience of solitude, travel, hunger and poverty; and the experience of serving others and even tending sheep. And amid these great experiences were smaller experiences of everyday life, various inner feelings, different kinds of thoughts and anxieties, new discoveries and information. Along with all this, it should also be remembered that Allah had endowed him with knowledge and wisdom as soon as he reached youth. (These experiences were made to undergo while he was in the position of a prince, taken out from that position.)

The truth is that the office of prophethood (*risalah*) is a duty and a great responsibility with many aspects, and manifold obligations fall upon the Prophet and the Messenger. Therefore it is extremely necessary for a Prophet to comprehend knowledge and excellence, wisdom and understanding, various experiences of life, and the practical lives of different people. And this practical experience is distinct from that theoretical knowledge and wisdom and from the divine revelation that is given to every Prophet, so that the conscience of the Prophet becomes pure and clean, and guidance is firmly placed in the heart of the Prophet.

From the history of the Messengers it becomes known that, apart from the missions entrusted to all the Prophets, the responsibilities of Musa (peace be upon him) were very heavy and difficult. He had to go before a rebellious and tyrannical ruler like Pharaoh. He was the greatest and wealthiest king of his era, the master of an ancient royal line. His government was extremely stable, and Egypt was then advanced in terms of civilisation and culture. He had reduced all the oppressed nations to slavery, and he held a high station on the earth.

Then Musa (peace be upon him) was sent for the liberation and migration of a people in whose hearts and minds slavery had taken root. They had become accustomed to a life of servitude, and their conscience had completely changed. They had in practice remained slaves for a very long time. The truth is that slavery corrupts human nature. Rot and stench arise within it, and such a people lose all sense of the filth, stench and rot. They cannot bear goodness, virtue, beauty and excellence. To raise such a corrupted people is a meaningful undertaking.

He was sent to a people who had once held the Islamic ideology from ancient times, but in whom a doctrinal deviation had arisen. In their hearts and minds that original, true form no longer existed. This people were neither upholding the old Islamic belief and Shariah, nor accepting the new belief properly. To reform such people is an extremely difficult task. To correct the crookedness within them, to straighten their deviation, and to remove the deep layers of superstition from their original beliefs were the most difficult aspects of this endeavour.

In brief, Musa was to build an entirely new community (*ummah*). From the very beginning, for the first time, he had to make the Children of Israel a distinct people, a people possessing a particular system, and a community bearing a particular messengership. And it is evident that building a people and a community is an extremely difficult task. This is why the Quran has repeated the story of Musa (peace be upon him) again and again. Because in the building of a new community upon the foundation of an ideology, the life of Musa (peace be upon him) was a specific model. In the path of such a great work there are internal and external difficulties. In such all-embracing calls, deviation also keeps arising. It also takes on specific forms, and it must pass through many experiences. And obstacles also come along the way.

The question is: why was Musa (peace be upon him) made to pass through the Bedouin-like life of Madyan? The answer is that this was so that he might also learn the ups and downs of the laborious life of common people and gain direct experience of it.

The life of royal palaces has a particular atmosphere, particular etiquettes and protocols. Even if someone is of sound nature, pure disposition, and possessed of knowledge and excellence, the shadow of palace life inevitably falls upon him, and some of its effects remain. As far as prophethood is concerned, a Messenger deals with the rich as well as with the poor. In the community there are wealthy people and there are poor people. Among them there are clean people and there are people who are dirty and unkempt, cultured people and savage people. There are people of pure nature and people of corrupt nature, good people and bad people, strong people and weak people, patient people and people who lament and wail. In short, the community contains every kind of person, and the Prophet has to reform them all. The poor have their own habits in eating, drinking, walking, and dress. They understand matters according to their own minds. They have a particular conception of life; their speech, their movements and gestures, their discourse and the manner of their awareness are of a distinct style. These common habits weigh very heavily upon those who were raised in palaces. People of lofty palaces do not even have the patience to look at the common manners of these people, let alone tolerate them and treat them. Although the hearts of these common people are full of goodness, and they are receptive to reform, because their outward manners and habits do not suit the one of the lofty palace.

A Messenger sometimes has to face hardships, solitude and poverty. But those who are accustomed to living in great palaces, however fervent their spirit of sacrifice may be, cannot endure poverty, deprivation and the hardships of practical life for a very long time, because they have become accustomed within palaces to luxury, abundance and ease.

Therefore, the will of Allah required that Musa (peace be upon him) be brought down a little from that high standard of palace life to the level of common life. He was to be placed within the society of shepherds, and after flight from fear, pursuit and the dread of being seized, he was to be accustomed to living the life of a shepherd, where he would receive only food and shelter. This was so that the arrogance that princes have toward poverty and the poor might be removed, and the aversion that princes harbour toward the habits, morals, roughness and simplicity of shepherds might be removed. So that Musa, the prince, would not consider himself exalted and distant from their ignorance, poverty, wretchedness and general ways. And so that he would be cast into the deep seas of common life, whereas previously he had been swimming within a limited stream of human life, so that he might be well prepared for the life of calling to the faith that lay ahead.

When the personality of Musa (peace be upon him) had completed these experiences and he became thoroughly familiar with the ups and downs of common life, and these experiences had come to him while living in another land as a stranger far from home, then the hand of divine power sent him back to the place of his birth, where his family and his people lived, and where he was to discharge the most difficult duty of prophethood. Now he is treading that same path. He had fled from it and had been running away completely alone. The question is: why did he come upon this same road and return? In fact, this was a kind of military exercise, intended to acquaint him with the ups and downs and the paths and passes of that road. Because the divine power had decided that soon Musa would lead his people along this very road into Sinai. This was in fact the training of every vanguard and leader, so that Musa would not need any other guide than himself, not even one to show him the way. For his people had fallen into a state in which they needed guidance in every matter, great and small, since humiliation, slavery and subjugation had utterly corrupted them. No reflection and no thought remained within them.

Now it has become clear how the divine power was training Musa (peace be upon him) under its own watchful eye, and how he was given excellent training for the performance of his prophetic duty. Now let us see how Musa undertook the journey of return.
